articles.content: Canada September CPI 3.1% y/y vs 3.2% expected US NAHB housing market index 29 vs 31 prior Bank of Canada Q3 business outlook survey -0.33 vs -0.38 prior CIBC cuts gold forecasts but still sees $5,500 in 2028 Oil reverses course higher after US and Houthi attacks Markets: S&P 500 up 0.4% WTI crude oil up $2.37 to $103.78 US 10-year yields up 4.2 bps to 5.14% AUD leads, JPY lags Gold down $25 to $4139 The AI trade rebounded on Monday as memory and chip names jumped on renewed optimism even as CoreWeave shares edged lower on debt worries. Amazon shares also jumped after an upgrade, gaining 5%. Despite that, decliner outnumbered advancers 2:1 so the breadth of the move was narrow. Part of the reason for that was an intraday reversal in oil prices. Crude started the week lower on Trump's waiving of sanctions on Russia but that move faded and then reversed on reports of small US strikes in Iran and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure. Oil finished the day solidly higher and that spilled over into bonds, with US 10s up 4 bps to 5.14%. US economic data was light but the NAHB numbers highlight how 2027 could be a rough year for the housing market if interest rates stay at these levels. In Canada, the loonie slipped after CPI numbers weren't as hot as expected. Despite that, RBC shifted its call to a BOC rate hike this month as central banks everywhere appeared to shift hawkishly at the IMF meetings, likely after sharing stories of broadening price pressures. Along those lines, the BOC survey of consumers showed rising 5-year inflation expectations. Finally, we are entering a period of intense election activity with eyes on the US midterms, Brazilian election, Israeli election and Canadian referendum. That's coming at the same time as the Q3 reporting calendar picks up. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Enforcement Notification - Tax fraud scheme using other taxpayers' personal information lands Laval man in prison
articles.desc: /CNW/ -- The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) announced today that Michel-Ange Bonny of Laval, Quebec, pleaded guilty to one count of fraud under the Criminal Code...
articles.content: Enforcement Notification - Tax fraud scheme using other taxpayers' personal information lands Laval man in prison /CNW/ -- The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) announced today that Michel-Ange Bonny of Laval, Quebec, pleaded guilty to one count of Code on October 5, 2026, at the Laval Courthouse. Mr. Bonny was sentenced to 18 months of imprisonment followed by a three-year probation order for the tax offence investigated by the CRA. Mr. Bonny was also facing other charges arising from a separate investigation conducted by the Laval Police Service for which a concurrent two-year prison sentence was imposed. As a result, Mr. Bonny will serve a total sentence of two years in prison for both offences. A CRA investigation revealed that Mr. Bonny orchestrated an identity-based tax scheme designed to fraudulently obtain tax refunds by using the personal information of other taxpayers to file false income tax returns and benefit returns (T1 returns) on their behalf. Between March and April 2019, 24 such returns for the 2018 tax year were filed without the knowledge or consent of the taxpayers involved. The returns included fictitious employment income and ineligible deductions to generate refunds to which the taxpayers were not entitled. It was confirmed that these filings were not authorized by the taxpayers, and that changes had been made to several of their CRA accounts without their knowledge, including mailing addresses and direct deposit information. The total amount of refunds fraudulently claimed was $226,809. Of that amount, $137,988 was deposited into the other taxpayers' bank accounts, by which Mr. Bonny personally benefited approximately $30,000. All case-specific information above was obtained from the court records. The CRA remains committed to combating tax evasion and other serious tax offences. There are significant consequences to breaking the law. Addressing tax evasion, tax is essential to protecting the integrity of Canada's tax system. While the vast majority of taxpayers comply with tax laws and meet their tax obligations, the CRA continues to administer a variety of programs aimed at protecting the fairness and integrity of the tax system. Cheating on your taxes affects the services and programs we all rely on to improve our quality of life. This is why the CRA works to ensure that individuals and businesses report all income earned and only claim benefits to which they are entitled, so that important benefit programs can be administered to those who need them. service to help Canadians stay current on the CRA's enforcement efforts. articles.title: EU Builds New Wall Against Chinese EVs While Korea Stands Exposed
articles.desc: The EU will limit EV subsidies to vehicles built in the bloc from 2028, while Korea keeps tariffs on Chinese cars at just 8%.
articles.content: EU Builds New Wall Against Chinese EVs While Korea Stands Exposed - Seoul Economic Daily The European Union is erecting new regulatory barriers to defend its market from a Chinese electric-vehicle offensive. Germany and France have agreed that from 2028, subsidies and public procurement benefits within the 27-nation bloc will go only to vehicles that are assembled and developed in the EU and that generate more than 70% of the value of core components excluding batteries, foreign media reported on the 18th. The aim is to tighten the "Made in Europe" standard, a policy favoring manufacturing inside the bloc, in order to block Chinese EVs entering the European market through detours such as Turkey. The EU also plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units a year starting in December, about half the current level. The EU is raising its defenses because China, armed with prices roughly 20% lower than European models, is threatening the bloc's manufacturing base. Chinese eco-friendly vehicles account for 12% of new car sales in Europe and are rapidly taking market share. In the global EV market outside China, Chinese brands including BYD held a 22.8% share from January through August. The United States has already imposed tariffs of up to 127.5% since 2024 to protect its home market from China's EV push. The EU levies tariffs of up to 45.3%, but has concluded that duties alone are not enough. With the U.S. and now the EU bolting the door against Chinese products, the Korean government has effectively done nothing. Tariffs on Chinese automobiles stand at just 8%, and taxpayer money is still handed out in purchase subsidies. Electric vehicles were also left out of the "Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act," which offers tax credits for domestic production in strategic industries. That leaves Korean companies defenseless against the export push by Chinese EV makers backed by massive state support. If this continues, the possibility cannot be ruled out that Korea's own EV market — of which 35% has already gone to Chinese brands — will be swallowed whole. The auto industry is a core strategic sector that underpins exports and employment, with wide ripple effects on upstream and downstream businesses. If it falters, the entire economy will take a critical hit as the manufacturing base weakens and jobs disappear. To fend off China's relentless EV offensive and preserve the competitiveness of a Korean auto industry now at a crossroads, the most urgent task is to include electric and hybrid vehicles in the Korean version of the IRA being pursued by the government and the National Assembly. articles.title: I Tried the 'Normatec Go' Compression Boots, and My Calves Have Never Felt Better
articles.desc: I can't imagine my recovery routine without them now.
articles.content: I Tried the 'Normatec Go' Compression Boots, and My Calves Have Never Felt Better | Lifehacker I Tried the 'Normatec Go' Compression Boots, and My Calves Have Never Felt Better I can't imagine my recovery routine without them now. Meredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more. We may earn a commission from links on this page. We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis. If you've ever been on your feet all day and your calves felt like two sandbags, you know how tough it can be to find relief. I'm a marathon runner, so I know it well. Training blocks mean high mileage, and calves take a beating on every mile. I've tried foam rollers, massage guns, stretching, and my favorite maneuver: lying with my This week's upgrade is the first recovery tool that seems to do all the work for me, and hey—after a long run, I'm not complaining. It's my first foray into compression boots: the Hyperice Normatec Go Calf - Recovery System with Patented Dynamic Compression Massage Technology (Normatec Go) FSA-HSA Approved How the Normatec Go compression boots work The Normatec Go is a pair of wearable compression sleeves that wrap around your calves and give you a dynamic air compression massage. Hyperice describes it as a fully portable version of its Normatec line, which pro athletes and recovery rooms have used for years. The sleeves inflate and deflate in a pulsing pattern (as opposed to just squeezing constantly). Hyperice calls this compression "gapless": There are three overlapping zones of 360-degree compression working through the calf. In theory, the wave of pressure helps push fluid and blood through your lower legs, which is why Hyperice says the massage increases circulation and reduces tension and swelling. Hyperice also points out that the calf is often called the body's "second heart" because it helps push blood back up from your lower legs. That matches my experience: After a long run, calves are where the heaviness and tightness show up first. The biggest upgrade over traditional compression boots is that you don't need to set up a whole system. You strap on the sleeves, open the app, pick an intensity, and relax. I've worn them at my desk, on the couch, and while answering emails after a long run. I show up to my next run feeling fresher, and for a marathon runner, that's the whole point of recovery. A few features make the experience better: Seven compression levels (40 to 200 mmHg), so you can go gentle after an easy run or firm after a long one The two sleeves always stay in sync for a symmetrical massage Bluetooth control through the Hyperice app, so you adjust everything from your phone 1.2 pounds total, and TSA friendly, so they can travel with you Hyperice recommends sessions of about 20 to 30 minutes. You can go up to 60 after a tough workout, or use a shorter 15- to 20-minute session at medium intensity before a run to warm up your legs. . Full-size compression boots that cover your whole leg usually run well , so that's a big difference. These only cover the calves, but if calves are where you need relief, you don't have to pay for coverage you won't use. They're also At the same time, the obvious limitation is that these are for calves only. I suppose it's a testament to the product that I've never been more tempted to spring for full-size boots, so that my quads and hamstrings can experience the same treatment. articles.title: New 3D form of carbon made in the lab
articles.desc: Like diamond, diamondiyne allotrope forms covalent bonds in three dimensions The post New 3D form of carbon made in the lab appeared first on Physics World.
articles.content: New 3D form of carbon made in the lab – Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account Researchers in Sweden have synthesized a new allotrope of carbon which, like diamond, forms covalent bonds in 3D. Unlike in diamond, however, carbon atoms in the new “diamondiyne” material form these bonds at relatively low pressure, producing a more porous crystal with properties that are still under investigation. Carbon is among the most versatile elements in the periodic table. Because it can bond with other elements in one, two or three dimensions, it is a building block for a wide range of structures with varying electronic properties. This versatility also appears when carbon bonds with itself to form allotropes such as fullerene (which is considered zero-dimensional, as its internal structure plays little role in its properties); one-dimensional carbon nanotubes; and two-dimensional graphite and graphene. The search for more carbon allotropes took off in 2004 after graphene was isolated for the first time. The number of theoretically predicted structures now stands at 1635, though most have never been created in the laboratory. Among those that have is an expanded version of graphene known as graphdiyne, which is composed of carbon atoms with different kinds of hybridized electronic orbitals (sp took the first steps towards making diamondiyne more than 30 years ago , getting to the final product proved challenging. The reasons are two-fold. First, one of the material’s building blocks, tetraethynylmethane, is unstable. Second, the carbon atoms in diamondiyne are covalently connected by robust single carbon–carbon bonds and even stronger triple carbon–carbon bonds. Such strong connections make it difficult to form a version of the material that is crystalline in all three dimensions. A cascade reaction on a liquid–liquid interface succeeded in producing the desired crystalline state using a so-called cascade reaction with kinetics they could control. This reaction takes place on a liquid–liquid interface, ensuring that monomers bind to a formed crystallite one by one. The result is an expanded crystal structure featuring a “carbo-mer” of diamond in which sp -hybridized carbons are connected by four sp-hybridized carbons to form two triple bonds – a structure commonly known as a ─diyne group. “To our knowledge, diamondiyne is the first allotrope besides diamond in which the carbon atoms form covalent bonds in all three dimensions,” Börjesson says. Liquid-liquid interfaces had previously been used to make graphdiyne and other 2D materials. In this work, the liquid–liquid system consisted of tetra(triethylsilylethynyl)methane and CuF ions in the latter molecule react with tetra(triethylsilylethynyl)methane, they produce tetraethynylmethane, which has exposed terminal alkyne groups – that is, structures containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond. The Cu ions then catalyse coupling between pairs of terminal alkynes. As the reaction proceeded, Börjesson and colleagues observed a film containing diamondiyne crystallites growing perpendicularly out of the interface between the two liquids. “We have previously shown that under such circumstances, the growth of covalent crystals is favoured kinetically,” Börjesson explains. To further encourage the emergence of the crystals via the molecule-by-molecule addition of tetraethynylmethane to the carbon film at the interface, Börjesson adds that the team kept the concentration of tetra(triethylsilylethynyl)methane relatively low. The finished films have an area of around 5 cm and are between several nanometres and tens of nanometres thick depending on the reaction time. articles.title: Watch This Snake Cartwheel Away From Danger
articles.desc: Keep on rolling The post Watch This Snake Cartwheel Away From Danger appeared first on Nautilus.
articles.content: Watch This Snake Cartwheel Away From Danger - Nautilus Watch This Snake Cartwheel Away From Danger , found in Southeast Asia, have a rather clever way of fleeing from trouble: They turn cartwheels until they’re safe from danger. See for yourself: Now, researchers have finally figured out how they do it, studying the action on video from multiple angles. Very precise, coordinated body movements keep the head of the snake stable and facing the direction of travel, while the rest of its body rotates. This gets around the main issue with rolling as a way of locomotion, as you’ll know if you’ve ever gone headfirst down a hill: It’s a real challenge to see where you’re going and keep traveling in the same direction. The faster the speed, the more difficult it gets, which isn’t ideal when you’re fleeing from predators. This Snake’s Tail Has a Fake “Spider” at the Tip With this method, snakes can move approximately 8 mph—four times faster than they can get around using traditional wriggling, and significantly faster than the average human jogger. Here are the particulars behind the movement: The part of the snake’s body in contact with the ground rolls and lifts the anterior portion of the snake, including the head, until the tip of its tail is the only part touching the floor. The tail then pushes off into a new loop, and the cycle continues. This isn’t the normal way of getting about for the dwarf reedsnake, but it does seem to come into play when they need to escape something in a hurry. In fact, the researchers say the snakes tended to dive underneath nearby objects for extra cover after rolling. We wouldn’t recommend such cartwheels when making your own quick getaways, though. Unless, maybe, you’re Buffy the Vampire Slayer. David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years.
